item.title: The Secret Health Benefits of Partner Touch in Older Couples
item.description:
Aging

The Secret Health Benefits of Partner Touch in Older Couples

A new study investigated the health benefits of partner touch

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Studies in younger people have shown substantial health benefits of social touch.
  • A new study investigated the health benefits of partner touch in older couples.
  • More frequent partner touch was linked to better cardiovascular and metabolic health five years later.
  • No effects were found for touch by other people.

For many people, life these days is increasingly stressful. One thing that can help deal with stress is feeling loved and cared for by partners, family members, and friends.

Indeed, it has been shown again and again in psychological research that social support can help in reducing stress and increasing psychological well-being. One of the most important forms of social support is social touch, such as hugging or hand holding (Ocklenburg, 2024).

Unfortunately, most of the psychological studies on the benefits of social touch have been conducted in younger volunteers. Understanding the benefits of social touch in older adults is thus an important gap in the psychological research literature.

What Are the Long-Term Effects of Partner Touch in Older Adults?

A new study, just published in the scientific journal Brain, Behavior, & Immunity–Health, turns the focus toward the long-term health effects of partner touch in older adults (Navyte et al., 2026). In the study, entitled “Long-term metabolic and cardiovascular health benefits from romantic partner touch in older adults,” the research team—led by scientist Gabriele Navyte from the University of Essex in the UK,—analyzed data from the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project.

Overall, 787 volunteers participated in the study. Their mean age was about 73 years, making this study cohort much older than the volunteers in most previous studies on partner touch and health.

All volunteers were tested two times, about five years apart, making it possible to investigate long-term health effects. About 70 percent of volunteers were in a relationship at the time point of the first data collection; the remaining 30 percent were single. At each time point, volunteers were asked how many times they had close physical contact with their partner in the preceding 12 months, and how many times they had close physical contact with other people who were not their partner in the preceding 12 months. The volunteers could answer on a scale between “never” to “once a month”, “once a week”, and ”several times a week or more.”

The physical health of the older volunteers was assessed across three categories:

  1. Metabolic health: Biomarkers related to important chemical reactions in cells
  2. Cardiovascular health: Heart health biomarkers like blood pressure or pulse
  3. Neuroendocrine health: Hormonal biomarkers

Partner Touch Had Unique Positive Effects on Older Adults

The scientists used sophisticated statistical models to investigate the effects of partner touch and touch by other people on health. Older adults who experienced more partner touch at the first time point had better metabolic and cardiovascular health at the second time point, five years later.

In contrast, touch by other people who were not the partner had no such positive effects on health. Moreover, no effects were found for neuroendocrine health.

Taken together, the results of the study suggest that in older adults, partner touch has a substantial positive association with various aspects of health, especially heart health, years later. These associations were not found for being touched by anybody else but the romantic partner. The scientists suggested that regular partner touch may be linked to lower chronic stress. The lower stress level may subsequently be linked to better cardiovascular and general health.

item.title: How Your Attachment Style Impacts You at Work
item.description:
Attachment

How Your Attachment Style Impacts You at Work

Why your attachment style impacts more than just your romantic relationships.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Attachment styles can shape how we handle stress and relationships at work.
  • Secure attachment is linked with lower burnout and job stress.
  • Anxious and avoidant attachment styles can make workplace stress harder to manage.

You may know about attachment styles when thinking about our bonds with parents, partners, children, and close friends. But attachment can also spill over into our work lives..

Attachment describes the ways we tend to think about ourselves and other people in close relationships. Broadly, attachment can be secure or insecure. Insecure attachment can take different forms, including anxious, avoidant-dismissive, and avoidant-fearful.

  • Secure attachment is linked with a more positive view of both yourself and others. You tend to trust that people can provide support and that you are worthy of support in return. You can enjoy closeness without needing constant reassurance, while also being comfortable with some distance.
  • Insecure attachment (anxious) tends to involve a more negative view of yourself and uncertainty about whether others can be trusted. You look to others for reassurance and validation. At work, this might show up as worrying about how your manager or colleagues view you, reading too much into a short email, or finding criticism especially hard to shake.
  • Insecure attachment (avoidant/dismissive) tends to involve a more positive view of yourself and a more negative view of others. You may place a high value on independence, avoid relying on others, and push down difficult emotions. At work, you might be reluctant to ask for help, keep colleagues at a distance, or pull back when you feel let down.
  • Insecure attachment (avoidant/fearful) combines both anxious and avoidant. You may want close relationships while also expecting that others will disappoint or hurt you. This can create a push-and-pull pattern—wanting connection, but feeling scared to connect because it feels too risky.
Source: Mikhail Nilov/Pexels

So, how does this impact me at work?

A meta-analysis on attachment and work found some interesting patterns. People with more secure attachment tended to report less burnout and job stress. Compared with those with anxious attachment that may have more trouble managing negative thoughts and emotions when faced with stress. Those with avoidant attachment may respond to disappointment by pulling away, which can make them less likely to ask for help.

Both patterns can make workplace stress harder to manage. And that matters because our work relationships can help us through stress and problems. So, unfortunately, both anxious and avoidant attached individuals tend to have lower job performance.

So what do we do?

If you have a more anxious attachment style, working with a leader who is consistent, clear, and supportive may help. If you tend to be more avoidant, finding a dependable leader who gives you space while still making support available may create a safer environment for you to engage.

If you are a leader, when an employee seems unusually worried, withdrawn, or reluctant to ask for help, it is worth looking at how you are showing up. Are expectations clear? Is feedback predictable? Do employees know where to go when they need support? Do you give people enough space while still staying connected?

We cannot—and should not—try to diagnose someone's attachment style at work. But understanding attachment can give us another lens for understanding workplace relationships.

Working toward greater awareness of your attachment style can help your career (as well as all of your relationships). More secure ways of relating can also help us handle stress, ask for support, give feedback, and build trust. And, research has found that securely attached individuals use more effective leadership styles, delegate more effectively, and are seen by followers as more natural leaders.

item.title: Superior Intelligence Is Here, and We Are at a Crossroads
item.description:
Intelligence

Superior Intelligence Is Here, and We Are at a Crossroads

When superior intelligence rules, what is the answer to this immense power?

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • We need to be talking about universal truths.
  • We now live in a world where superior intelligence is an all-encompassing reality.
  • Neuroscience indicates there are no shortcuts to how the human brain functions.
Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

We need to talk about universal truths. One such truth, from a psychological perspective, is that if a problem is ignored or denied, it will continue to be a problem. Issues, problems, and concerns need to be the cobblestones that build the road of knowledge and construction rather than self-destruction.

Today, we live in a world where artificial intelligence is all-encompassing. Because of what artificial intelligence is achieving, it has been referred to as “super intelligence.” However, given what AI (without human intervention) is achieving independently, which surpasses what humans are realizing, a more universally accurate descriptor for AI now may need to be that of “superior intelligence.”

Superior Intelligence Rules

Empirical evidence suggests that superior intelligence (SI) is already a significant, dominant, and even intrusive force across many organizational operations.

The present empirical internet indicators suggest that humanity is now on the cusp of not only losing the capacity to control its current organizational, social, and internet circumstances, but it also seems to be at the early stages of also losing control of its immediate internet-based structural and social future.

This civilizational dilemma is inseparable from the developmental foundations of human agency. If SI shapes childhood environments through device immersion, it will, as the neuroscience already informs, reshape the very neurological and social conditions required for human autonomy, personal and social responsibility, and rational choice to take place.

The Universal Dilemma of Machine Domination

Neuroscience indicates there are no shortcuts to how the human brain functions, which gives rise to consciousness, the mind, cognition, and free will.

As Claxton (2015) points out, the body and brain “is designed to blend all” internal and external “influences together” into one seamless operating entity for the purpose of achieving holistic efficiencies and operational excellence.

As such, it is important to note here that the emergence of consciousness is what helped to develop, advance, and enhance cognition, motor learning, self-reflective intellectual insights, skills, knowledge, critical thinking, and higher-order reasoning, which eventually created the physical world in which we now live. And in relation to what is now taking place, this now includes the intrusive, independently dominant, superior machine-based reality of superior intelligence.

To universally deal with this, we need to make sure that our education system is operating in a manner that advances critical thinking and higher-order reasoning in accordance with how the human brain functions, which then lead to the outcomes of meritorious achievements, competence, and universal standards of recognized excellence. However, the evidence now informs this is not taking place.

Educational Standards, Physical Play, Universal Truths

Recent data on educational outcomes indicate that academic standards in America and Australia are declining alongside increased technology use. Additional research also indicates that moral, ethical, empathetic, and Theory of Mind capacities appear to be declining (ACARA, 2026; Alexopoulos, 2025; Chai & Wang, 2025; Rogelberg, 2026).

Research suggests that, from a very early age, toddlers and children are engaging with devices. As soon as this happens, they stop moving, babbling, and talking, plus they also stop engaging face-to-face with others and their external world, both visually and auditorily. Consequently, they are no longer culturally engaged with their family or with society (Christakis et al., 2009; Linebarger & Vaala, 2010).

Crucially, device use and gaming are not play. Through play, that must involve physical play, the brain, mind, emotions, imagination, and ethical and moral social development occur.

Profoundly, play is the immutable, genetically based, universal developmental process that holistically develops the brain, mind, and body for eventual adulthood, including the development of agency, insightful autonomy, plus moral, ethical, empathetic, and Theory of Mind development (Ginsburg et al., 2007; Yogman et al., 2018).

Moral, Ethical, Empathetic, and Theory of Mind Development

Regarding moral, ethical, empathetic and Theory of Mind development (which require continuous human interaction from birth onward), disruption of this holistic trajectory leads to outcomes that negatively affect the brain, mind, body, emotions, and the psychological, physical, social, moral and ethical development of the universal human condition (Alexopoulos, 2025; Chai & Wang, 2025).

This negative impact now appears regularly in research and the media. Research indicates that some teenagers and even children are acting out more violently. This suggests that their holistic social, ethical, and moral development have not matured as required. Research suggests that these children and adolescents are making their negative choices that may be linked to their ongoing immersion in device use (Browne & Hamilton-Giachritsis, 2005; Munthe & de Fine Licht, 2014; Wilson, 2008).

When device immersion replaces human interaction, research indicates that this choice disrupts the neurological developmental conditions necessary for moral, ethical, empathetic, and Theory of Mind reasoning, which are the capacities that underpin human autonomy and responsible moral choices and an ethical civil society. As such morals, ethics, empathy, and Theory of Mind are absolutely required of adults (Alexopoulos, 2025; Chai & Wang, 2025; Purje, 2014).

Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

October 1962

In relation to morality, ethics, empathy, and Theory of Mind, let’s look to history for lessons. For the second time in history, humanity stands at the crossroads of civilization's continuation. The first occurred during the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962.

During this time, the political leaders made choices that could have resulted in a nuclear conflagration. However, before that happened, they made political, moral, ethical, empathetic, and Theory of Mind-driven choices that averted this outcome. The Cuban Missile Crisis began and ended because those in power talked and universally agreed on the immensely complex political and the associated universal ethical and moral nuances.

October 2026

Approaching October 2026, we are again, for what seems like a second time, at a crossroads that involves civilization’s destiny. Human consciousness gives us the intellectual capacity for choice and free will, which brought humanity to both crossroads. It was human consciousness, coupled with the development of moral, ethical, empathetic, Theory of Mind, and higher-order reasoning, that solved the first issue. We absolutely need this to take place now.

When we examine history, we often use the “what if” scenario. This “what if” use is purely academic and deepens insight into what might have happened if we had made a different decision.

However, once we examine the “what if,” we advance knowledge, and yet, self-evidently, the historical outcome remains unchanged. We cannot change history; we can only change what we do now. Choices have consequences. Choose wisely (Purje, 2014). The mythology surrounding Pandora’s box endures for a reason.

item.title: What to Do When Your Personal Battery is at 15%
item.description:
Burnout

What to Do When Your Personal Battery is at 15%

Ways to cope when you're feeling chronically drained.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Our lives are so full that many say they are perpetually in a state of feeling drained.
  • Identifying that perpetually drained feeling is a first step.
  • We offer suggestions, to tailor to your life, that can help.

You know that feeling when your cell phone's battery is at 15 percent? It's still working, but the indicator is red and you don’t know how much longer you have before it stops.

I'm guessing that you have had times in your life when you felt like you were at 15 percent, too. You were still functioning but your indicator was red and you weren't sure how much longer you had until you were drained.

We can manage this kind of drained state for a while, but we can’t keep it up forever. It is uncomfortable, both because we do not know when our energy will fade completely and because, unlike a phone, when our energy is at 15 percent, it's just harder to carry out everyday functions. We will have to plug in to recharge somehow.

Are You Running on Empty?

Indicators of a chronic drained state include:

  • feeling emotionally or physically tired (or both) day after day
  • having repeated thoughts like “it can’t go on like this” while knowing you have to continue to complete the daily functions of life
  • having to consistently push yourself with the thought “I just need to keep putting one foot in front of the other.”
  • having a shorter fuse than you usually have. Even when you don’t lose your temper you notice that small inconveniences feel more annoying than they should.
  • starting every day thinking about what is between you and getting into bed that evening.

And of course, this list is not exhaustive.

Living in a chronically drained state is problematic for a number of reasons:

  • It is hard to maintain. It's one thing if you know that you are going through a temporary and finite period. You just have to get through it. It is another if there is no end in sight.
  • It has the potential to harm relationships. When you're feeling drained, you're likely to be shorter-tempered and more irritable than usual.
  • It puts you at risk for burnout. You may find yourself detaching from your job, your relationships, and the other activities that bring you meaning and joy.

Perhaps the key to solving the chronic 15% drained state is similar to what you might do to solve the 15% left on your cell phone: Find ways to recharge, and if they aren’t working, do a deeper dive to find out if there is another problem. Think about the following:

  • Make sure you are taking care of yourself at a basic physical and emotional level. For example, make sure you are sleeping as much as you need and eating decently
  • While your energy is low, think about what you may be able to let go of or, if you have the means, outsource. What can be done in ways that take less time and energy, such as ordering groceries on-line rather than going to the supermarket? To continue the analogy, maybe delete some apps.
  • What fills your cup rather than drains it? Do you need to find a few minutes to connect with that dear old friend? Can you carve out 10 minutes of quiet time? Would it help to write something into your schedule that you are looking forward to doing and try to protect that time? Do you need to remember routines that feel grounding, but have gone by the wayside?
  • Reach out for help. Who in your life can give you a little relief, help you take care of something that needed taking care of, or listen to you vent for a bit without trying to solve what may be unsolvable problems?
  • Think about if there may be a bigger problem to solve. Consider psychotherapy. Nobody deserves to be left with that 15 percent feeling.

This chronic drained feeling is not uncommon. Life, for many of us, has gotten so full and some raise the skill of filling their schedule to an art form.

There is an analogy about filling a bucket with rocks and then, once you think it is full, adding pebbles. When, again, you think it is full, pour in the sand. Lest you think it is full then, try adding water!

I (JS) can never remember the point of that analogy. Upon looking it up, I have seen a couple of messages—including that we should think about the biggest rocks as our top priorities, the pebbles as our next-level priorities, and so on down. That second one is closer to my takeaway: “Then it's too heavy to lift!” Lots of us keep trying to lift it, and we may do a passable job. However, it gets really hard.

We need to recognize when it has been too heavy for too long—when we have been tolerating staying at 15 percent for a while, noticing the red indicator and worrying that we will shut off, but staying right there. Spend a little bit of the energy left figuring out how to recharge. Life feels better on a full battery.

item.title: When Disappointment Feels Like Betrayal
item.description:
Relationships

When Disappointment Feels Like Betrayal

Disappointment is part of daily living; betrayal should never occur.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • In love relationships, self-doubt—fed by disappointment—fosters negative judgments of partners.
  • Conflating disappointment and betrayal is a potent polarizing force in love.
  • In polarized relationships, both partners often feel judged, unsupported, and gaslit.

What’s amazed me in the past decade of work with distressed couples is the degree to which polarization—with its disdain for alternative perspectives and compromise and its conspicuous intolerance and readiness to condemn—has infected committed relationships. Partners sound more like fractious lawyers arguing cases than lovers desiring reconciliation.

Polarization in love relationships goes well beyond the relatively uncommon occurrence of a progressive partner married to a conservative. In love relationships, polarization takes the form of a general demand that partners think, feel, and behave alike. This is tragically ironic as we tend to seek out partners with different temperaments to “fill in our gaps.” In polarized relationships, the differences that initially attracted partners become signals of betrayal.

Polarized relationships are all but doomed because partners almost always give different emotional meaning to the same events and behaviors. The meaning we assign to events and behaviors rises from temperament, personal history, and metabolism, all of which differ in partners.

In polarized relationships, both partners feel judged and gaslit, unable to have their own thoughts, feelings, and behavior choices. Both feel they are asked to sell out the self to save the relationship.

Nowhere is the crisis of polarization in love relationships more evident than the conflation of disappointment and betrayal, that is, when disappointed partners feel betrayed.

The only way to avoid disappointment is to have no desires, preferences, or expectations, which sounds like a description of depression. How well we do in love depends on how we respond to disappointment, whether we blame, deny, or avoid or try to improve, appreciate, connect, or protect.

It’s crucial to the health of relationships—and to personal well-being—to keep disappointment distinct from betrayal.

Disappointment vs. Betrayal

Disappointment frustrates preferences—what we hope or wish for; betrayal violates values, especially good faith and trust.

We trust loved ones never to hurt us intentionally; we prefer that loved ones never hurt us at all, even unintentionally.

We trust loved ones to maintain love, compassion, and faithful behavior; we prefer that loved ones never feel attracted to anyone else.

We trust loved ones to accept and value us for whom we are; we prefer that loved ones share all our opinions, tastes, and preferences.

We trust loved ones to support and appreciate us; we prefer that loved ones think we’re smart, attractive, talented, successful.

We trust loved ones to want us to be happy; we prefer that loved ones make us happy.

We must distinguish disappointment from betrayal to achieve happiness in close relationships. Share your core emotions—fear, shame, or sadness—and not coping mechanisms of blame, denial, or avoidance. Coping tactics drive us apart; core emotions bring us together.

item.title: Pygmalion: The Greek Myth Warning of Parasocial Love
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

Pygmalion: The Greek Myth Warning of Parasocial Love

Greek mythology offers a timely warning about losing touch with reality.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Pygmalion's love for his statue warns against losing touch with reality via fantasy or ideals.
  • Parasocial relationships offer illusory intimacy but lack real emotional reciprocity.
  • Social media and AI amplify risks of unrealistic attachments and emotional isolation.

Fall is the perfect time to go within, refresh your routine, and engage your senses. Perhaps you take notice of the autumnal leaves, engage in novelty, or even travel.

This change of season, this "newness," shatters the illusion that your current life is the only possible reality. Much like the myth of Pygmalion, we can easily lose touch with ourselves by getting caught up in the noise of this artificial world. This cautionary tale warns us of the heavy toll we pay—losing our identity and blurring healthy boundaries—when we let the noise of the world isolate us from our true selves.

Source: Zeeshaan Shabbir, used with permission

The Story of Pygmalion

Pygmalion was a highly skilled and widely admired sculptor in Greek mythology. Disheartened by what he perceived as the imperfections of mortal women, he gave up pursuit of them and took a vow of celibacy. Instead, he dedicated himself to a life of art and creation and set out to create an artistic representation of the ideal female form. From the finest ivory, the sculptor devoted himself to chiseling every feature with increasing care and tenderness.

After many months, he transformed an already fine figure into one of unrivaled beauty—with refined features, radiant ivory skin, long windswept locks, and a generous waist-hip ratio. These visual signals of health and fertility remain timeless symbols of female beauty. He named his masterpiece Galatea.

Once completed, the sculpture was so exquisitely beautiful that he fell deeply in love with it. The artwork was so lifelike that Pygmalion would touch it to confirm that it was not a living being. He progressed from admiring the sculpture to murmuring to it, caressing it, and even kissing it with his eyes closed. He envisioned her coming to life in his embrace. He was passionately in love with his own creation. He bestowed upon the statue gifts, dressed it in luxurious silks, undressed it, and even took it to bed.

According to the myth, Pygmalion prayed to the goddess Aphrodite on her festival day, his voice trembling with hope as he beseeched her to bring his beloved statue to life, longing for the warmth of a heartbeat and the spark of true love to awaken within the marble form he had crafted with such devotion. The Greek goddess of love, beauty, and desire was often described as charming, alluring, and enchanting. She was known for her irresistible beauty and her ability to inspire love and passion in others. Aphrodite was believed to embody love in all its forms, from romantic love to physical desire, and was associated with grace, elegance, and sensuality. When she encountered those truly devoted to love, she was known to show compassion, intervene, and even bestow blessings.

Pygmalion begged her to bring his beloved masterpiece to life, pleading for the “living likeness of my ivory girl." Aphrodite was moved by Pygmalion's pure and devoted love for Galatea. As a reward for his sincerity and passion, she brought the statue to life. When Pygmalion returned home, he kissed his beloved statue on the lips, as he always had. But this time, he was astonished to feel warmth and tenderness in the embrace. He could feel the pulse of sweet Galatea's lips as she began to return his kiss. The more he touched and caressed her, the more she came to life. Eventually, she opened her hazel eyes for the first time. Startled at first, she grew overjoyed by the sight of her devoted lover and reciprocated his ardor. With the blessing of Aphrodite, Pygmalion and Galatea were happily wed, and eventually they had a son.

Pygmalion had treated his statue like a real person. He spoke tenderly to Galatea, caressed her, and brought her thoughtful gifts. To him, she had become so much more than a statue carved from ivory; she became in his eyes the personification of the ideal woman. The myth has the couple living happily ever after. But in real life, Pygmalion's behavior would not lead to a happy ending.

Pygmalion's Fixation With Galatea Represents a Lack of Healthy Boundaries

Pygmalion lived in a trance, losing touch with the division between fantasy and reality. He put up emotional walls with real women that kept him in isolation; he lacked real emotional connection with the outer world, and clearly had difficulties in forming close relationships with real-life humans. His unrealistic ideals and disdain for women led him down the path of neglecting the need for authentic human connections. Many artists can empathize with this emotional journey of becoming so captivated by their creation that they immerse themselves in their inner world, forsaking the external world for the beauty of their imaginative ideals. This type of infatuation within the context of a "parasocial" relationship raises concerns about the dangers of losing touch with reality and getting lost in an illusion.

In today's world, a parasocial relationship is a one-sided, psychological bond that a lonely and isolated person may form with a media persona, celebrity, or public figure. In this type of relationship, the individual feels a sense of connection, attachment, or intimacy with the media personality, even though there is no actual interaction or personal relationship between them. This phenomenon is commonly observed in fandoms, where fans develop emotional connections with celebrities or characters they admire through media platforms like television, social media, or events. Parasocial relationships can have both positive and negative impacts on individuals, influencing their emotions, behaviors, and perceptions of the public figure involved. Ultimately, however, the relationship will feel hollow because it is inherently one-sided. The object of your affection isn't going to call you on your birthday or laugh with you about the smaller absurdities of life. The intimacy is an illusion.

In the age of AI, social media, and increased accessibility to celebrities, individuals can develop unrealistic expectations about their favorite personalities, leading to disappointment when those expectations are not met in reality. Parasocial relationships can allow people to connect without the risks associated with real-life interactions. They can offer a sense of vicarious companionship without the fear of real-life rejection or vulnerability. Emotional walls are constructed from bricks of self-protection and isolation, bound together by the cement of fear. They may create a mirage of safety, but ultimately relational trauma needs relational repair. One of the greatest psychological detriments of our time is the rise of parasocial relationships. Take time to step into what is real.

And remember…

Individuals who understand the importance of boundaries are self-healers. Akin to alchemists, they possess the remarkable ability to transform wounds into wisdom, pain into purpose, and mistreatment from others into opportunities for assertive self-advocacy. This year, I urge you to put down the phone and really connect with the person next to you. Forget the illusions of the online world. Say no to what feels parasocial and lean into those small nameless moments that are real.

item.title: Beware AI-Generated Scams
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Beware AI-Generated Scams

Unforeseen consequences abound when considering AI "slop" is everywhere.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • AI-generated tools pose significant threats.
  • Public erosion continues to deteriorate with AI "slop."
  • Who is responsible when AI tools impersonate public figures?

This week, I received what appeared on the surface to be two extremely promising emails regarding a recent book of mine that was published (e.g., Aalai, 2026). Imagine my surprise when one of my favorite authors—who I have never met before—sent me a glowing email about this newest book of mine, full of personal anecdotes and reasons why she was drawn to the text. After recovering from the surprise of seeing her name in my inbox, it didn’t take me long to surmise that the message I had received was not, in fact, from the author Kristin Hannah, but was entirely AI-generated (this would later be confirmed by a response from her PR team, when I forwarded them the suspicious email).

AI has been making headlines for years now, but in particular this week with some of the most powerful political leaders convening at the U.N. Moreover, the current U.S. president hosted a dinner for China’s leader that boasted seemingly all of the richest men in the world—with a disproportionate number of Big Tech bros, many of them the architects of the AI-powered tools that have been foisted upon the masses. Readers who have followed my posts here, or who are familiar with my most recent book, Disconnection: The Search for Identity in a Digital Age, are familiar with the skepticism I have shared regarding the extent to which the newest AI innovations will serve to improve the majority of users’ lives.

The irony is not lost on me that one of my work emails have been trolled by AI-powered tools for the very book that has raised concerns about these innovations—dedicating an entire chapter to warning readers about how AI is the atomic bomb of our century. Moreover, I have no idea who—if anyone—was behind the recent email messages I received that were AI-generated, or why. As I recovered from these false communications, I started to think about how it impacts users when communications they are led to believe are being driven by a human on the other side of their device is in fact a bot, or driven by an AI-powered tool.

Who Is Accountable for AI Impersonation?

Moreover, I couldn’t help but wonder: who is responsible for impersonating an author, and leading another writer to believe they were the recipient of their praise and engagement? Eng & Yan (2026) have identified through their research that people do believe machines are capable of engaging in wrongdoing, and that not surprisingly, they experience lower levels of justice satisfaction after “punishing” machines compared to humans. In my case, that wasn’t even an option, as I don’t know why I was targeted, and who or what entity may have been behind it. Is it possible that AI systems went “rogue” on their own, and specifically targeted an author who has written extensively warning of the dangers of these very creations?

This incident points to yet another unforeseen risk of a digital landscape that is increasingly being run by AI-powered tools—namely, in a culture which is already overrun by a diffusion of responsibility at the highest level of power and political leadership, users who are the targets of the kind of communications I received this week are left on their own to grapple with the fallout. My relatively high media literacy, in addition to the fact that I am regularly scanning documents into programs to detect whether writing is AI-generated or not for purposes of grading student performance (a sad reality, indeed), left me far less vulnerable to believing the messages I received this week were authentic. I can’t help but wonder, however, what may have developed had I responded to the message from this alleged author, and enabled the correspondence to continue.

Calls for Regulation and the Scale of AI Risks

Given that the creators behind some of the largest corporations developing AI-tools have testified at the U.N. this week imploring some form of global order or regulation for these fast-spreading tools, it goes without saying that my personal experiences this week have been tame relative to the damage these tools are capable of.

Nonetheless, the experiences I have shared here point to a dangerous new reality: any form of digital communication now lends itself to susceptibility for exploitation and infiltration by AI-generated tools. How is this going to impact the already-eroding public trust many Americans are feeling today, when we don’t even know if we can trust the messages showing up in our very own inboxes?

item.title: 10 Ways People Can Manipulate You and How to Recognize It
item.description:
Persuasion

10 Ways People Can Manipulate You and How to Recognize It

Healthy influence leaves room to choose. Manipulation does not.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Manipulation interferes with your ability to decide freely, unlike healthy influence.
  • Tactics like fear, guilt, and shame can signal manipulation, not normal persuasion.
  • Isolation and controlling information deepen dependence on the manipulator.

We influence each other all the time. A friend asks you to come to dinner. Your romantic partner tells you they’re hurt by something you did. A salesperson talks your ear off about a car you are considering. A politician promises you the moon.

When do these forms of influence become manipulation?

While there is no single agreed-upon definition of manipulation in the literature, a key part of many definitions is that manipulation is a form of influence that interferes significantly with a person’s ability to decide for themselves. That is, when somebody uses aspects of another person’s psychology, such as their emotions, vulnerabilities, needs, or cognitive tendencies in ways that interfere with that person’s ability to think and decide for themselves.

Though some manipulative techniques are obvious, many are subtle, as we shall see in the next section.

10 ways influence can become manipulation

Before I describe the 10 forms of influence, note that none is a sure sign that you are being manipulated. There is a continuum, in a sense, from ordinary interpersonal influence to increasingly controlling or abusive patterns.

What matters is how these tactics are used, what alternatives the person leaves you with, and more importantly, to what extent these tactics are being used to interfere with your ability to think and decide things autonomously.

As you will see, these tactics work through different psychological, social, behavioral, and informational mechanisms.

1. Fear

Using fear to make refusal feel unsafe or very costly. This can be done through threats, intimidation, violence, or exaggerated warnings about what will happen if you do not do as they demand.

2. Guilt

Making you feel responsible for their suffering or problems that you are either not actually responsible for or for which you do not have as much responsibility as they claim.

3. Obligation

Taking advantage of your sense of obligation so that refusing feels wrong. Remember, this is not about ordinary feelings of obligation, but about situations where that obligation is exaggerated, one-sided, or simply irrelevant to the situation.

4. Shame

Using shame to make you feel that refusing would prove you are selfish, immoral, defective, ridiculous, or just a very, very terrible person.

5. Withdrawing affection

Using affection, approval, or the threat of losing the relationship to make compliance feel like the price of being loved or accepted. This might involve them withdrawing affection, threatening abandonment, or unexpectedly showering you with excessive affection, as can happen with some forms of love bombing.

6. Isolation

Cutting you off from friends, family, co-workers, or other sources of support, making you more and more dependent on the manipulator and less likely to meet people who might challenge their influence. This can be particularly vicious.

7. Social pressure

This one is about alliances, about recruiting friends, relatives, co-workers, or other members of your social group to take their side and use social approval to pressure you.

8. Surveillance and monitoring

Monitoring your movements, communications, relationships, spending, and pretty much every aspect of your behavior so that you begin watching and policing yourself to avoid their displeasure. In a way, you feel their presence all the time, even when they are not there.

9. Controlling the information

Controlling or distorting the information available to you through lies, misleading claims, "convenient" omissions, etc. As a result, your ability to make an informed decision is significantly reduced and their preferred conclusion seems the only reasonable course of action.

10. Undermining your judgment

This is another vicious one and involves undermining your confidence in your ability to perceive, remember, interpret, or evaluate situations accurately, so that you become increasingly dependent on their version of events. See my post on gaslighting.

Takeaway

Healthy relationships involve influence. We ask for things, negotiate, persuade, compromise, and sometimes even become a little pushy. I hope this information can help you spot manipulation more easily. The goal, however, should not be hypervigilance and paranoia, just as blind trust is dangerous, but striking a balance so you can recognize when someone's influence begins to undermine your ability to think and decide autonomously.

So it is useful to remember that when someone increasingly makes fear, guilt, shame, dependence, isolation, or other forms of pressure the price of refusing them, it is reasonable to suspect we are moving away from ordinary persuasion and into the territory of manipulation. So the alarms should be going off.

Sometimes, the first sign of manipulation is just realizing that saying “no”—or even thinking it—does not feel like a genuine option. As someone told me, “It’s like walls are closing in and the only way out is to do what they want. That’s when I know. When the question is not what I want. Not even if I will give in… but when.”

When that happens, creating some distance and breathing room can give you a chance to think about the situation without immediate pressure. And if this is something you are being subjected to repeatedly, talking with a mental health professional could be a good idea. They could help you understand what is happening, think through your options, and work on setting more effective boundaries. If you are experiencing manipulation or abuse, you don't have to deal with it alone. Help is available.
